Drafts can be divided into two broad subcategories: sight drafts and time drafts. 
 
A sight draft calls for payment “on sight,” that is, when presented. Recall from Section 19.1 
"Introduction to Commercial Paper" that Lorna Love wished to buy tennis rackets from Rackets, Inc. 
Suppose Love had the money to pay but did not want to do so before delivery. Rackets, on the other hand, 
did not want to ship before Love paid. The solution: a sight draft, drawn on Love, to which would be 
attached an order bill of lading that Rackets received from the trucker when it shipped the rackets. The 
sight draft and bill of lading go to a bank in Love’s city. When the tennis rackets arrive, the carrier notifies 
the bank, which presents the draft to Love for payment. When she has done so, the bank gives Love the 
bill of lading, entitling her to receive the shipment. The bank forwards the payment to Rackets’ bank, 
which credits Rackets’ account with the purchase amount. 
 
A time draft, not surprisingly, calls for payment on a date specified in the draft. Suppose that Love will 
not have sufficient cash to pay until she has sold the rackets but that Rackets needs to be paid 
immediately. The solution: a common form of time draft known as a trade acceptance. Rackets, the seller, 
draws a draft on Love, who thus becomes a drawee. The draft orders Love to pay the purchase price to the

A second type of commercial paper is the common bank check, a special form of draft. Section 3-104(2)(b) 
of the UCC defines a check as “a draft drawn on a bank and payable on demand.” Postdating a check 
(putting in a future date) does not invalidate it or change its character as payable on demand. Postdating 
simply changes the first time at which the payee may demand payment. Checks are, of course, usually 
written on paper forms, but a check can be written on anything—a door, a shirt, a rock—though certainly 
the would-be holder is not obligated to accept it. 
 
Like drafts, checks may be accepted by the drawee bank. Bank acceptance of a check is 
called certification; the check is said to be certified by stamping the word “certified” on the face of the 
check. When the check is certified, the bank guarantees that it will honor the check when presented. It can 
offer this guarantee because it removes from the drawer’s account the face amount of the check and holds 
it for payment. The payee may demand payment from the bank but not from the drawer or any prior 
indorser of the check. 
A certified check is distinct from a cashier’s check. A cashier’s check is drawn on the account of the 
bank itself and signed by an authorized bank representative in return for a cash payment to it from the 
customer. The bank guarantees payment of the cashier’s check also.

A note—often called a promissory note—is a written promise to pay a specified sum of money on 
demand or at a definite time. There are two parties to a note: the maker (promisor), and 
the payee (promisee). For an example of a promissory note, see Figure 19.4 "A Promissory Note". The 
maker might execute a promissory note in return for a money loan from a bank or other financial 
institution or in return for the opportunity to make a purchase on credit.

qa_pairs.answer: A check, being a specific type of draft defined under the Uniform Commercial Code as a 'draft drawn on a bank and payable on demand,' can be accepted by the drawee bank. When a check is certified, it means the bank guarantees that it will honor the check upon presentation, having already removed the face amount from the drawer’s account. Accommodation Party 
An accommodation party is one who signs a negotiable instrument in order to lend her name to 
another party to the instrument. It does not matter in what capacity she signs, whether as maker or 
comaker, drawer or codrawer, or indorser. As a signatory, an accommodation party is always a surety 
(Chapter 23 "Legal Aspects of Banking"; a surety is one who guarantees payment if the primarily obligated 
party fails to pay). The extent of the accommodation party’s liability to pay depends on whether she has 
added language specifying her purposes in signing. Section 3-416 of the UCC distinguishes between a 
guaranty of payment and a guaranty of collection. An accommodation party who adds words such as 
“payment guaranteed” subjects herself to primary liability: she is guaranteeing that she will pay if the 
principal signatory fails to pay when the instrument is due. But if the accommodation party signs 
“collection guaranteed,” the holder must first sue the maker and win a court judgment. Only if the 
judgment is unsatisfied can the holder seek to collect from the accommodation party. When words of 
guaranty do not specify the type, the law presumes a payment guaranty.

The modern law of commercial paper is, in general, covered by UCC Article 3. The two basic types of

qa_pairs.question: What does an accommodation party do and what is their liability under different conditions?
qa_pairs.answer: An accommodation party is someone who signs a negotiable instrument to assist another party, regardless of their role as maker, comaker, drawer, codrawer, or indorser. They act as a surety, meaning they guarantee payment if the primarily obligated party fails to pay. Their liability depends on the wording added during the signing. If the accommodation party writes 'payment guaranteed,' they assume primary liability, promising to pay the debt if the principal signatory defaults. Conversely, if they write 'collection guaranteed,' the holder must first sue the maker and secure a court judgment before seeking the accommodation party's payment. In cases where the wording is ambiguous, the law assumes a payment guaranty.

qa_pairs.question: Why must the value of a negotiable instrument be ascertainable from its face, without extrinsic reference?
qa_pairs.answer: The requirement that the value of a negotiable instrument be ascertainable from its face, without extrinsic reference, is set forth in the UCC and ensures that the instrument's terms and conditions are clear and unambiguous, allowing for immediate and direct transferability. This rule prevents ambiguity and ensures that parties can rely solely on the document itself for understanding its terms, thus facilitating efficient financial transactions and reducing the need for additional documentation or clarification.

qa_pairs.question: What are the six requirements for an instrument to meet the negotiability test?
qa_pairs.answer: According to the UCC, for an instrument to meet the negotiability test, it must satisfy the following six requirements: 1) It must be in writing; 2) It must be unconditional and signed by the maker; 3) It must promise to pay a fixed amount of money; 4) It must be payable on demand or at a definite time; 5) It must be payable to order or to bearer; 6) It must be transferred by delivery or endorsement. These requirements ensure that the instrument is capable of being transferred and serves as a reliable medium for financial transactions.

Summary 
Commercial paper is the collective term for a variety of instruments—including checks, certificates of 
deposit, and notes—that are used to pay for goods; commercial paper is basically a contract to pay money. 
The key to the central role of commercial paper is negotiability, the means by which a person is 
empowered to transfer to another more than what the transferor himself possesses. The law regulating 
negotiability is Article 3 of the Universal Commercial Code. 
 
Commercial paper can be divided into two basic types: the draft and the note. A draft is a document 
prepared by a drawer ordering the drawee to remit a stated sum of money to the payee. Drafts can be 
subdivided into two categories: sight drafts and time drafts. A note is a written promise to pay a specified 
sum of money on demand or at a definite time. 
 
A special form of draft is the common bank check, a draft drawn on a bank and payable on demand. A 
special form of note is the certificate of deposit, a written acknowledgment by a bank that it has received 
money and agrees to repay it at a time specified in the certificate. 
 
In addition to drawers, makers, drawees, and payees, one can deal with commercial paper in five other 
capacities: as indorsers, indorsees, holders, holders in due course, and accommodation parties. 
A holder of a negotiable instrument must be able to ascertain all essential terms from its face. These terms 
are that the instrument (1) be in writing, (2) be signed by the maker or drawer, (3) contain an 
unconditional promise or order to pay (4) a sum certain in money, (5) be payable on demand or at a 
definite time, and (6) be payable to order or to bearer. If one of these terms is missing, the document is 
not negotiable, unless it is filled in before being negotiated according to authority given.

qa_pairs.question: Why might handwriting be preferred over printing or typing on negotiable instruments like checks?
qa_pairs.answer: Handwriting provides a level of personalization and authenticity that can help prevent fraud. When a person writes their name on a negotiable instrument, it is harder to forge compared to printed names. This handwritten signature serves as a unique identifier that can be recognized by the bank and the recipient, adding an extra layer of security. Additionally, if there are alterations or discrepancies, the handwriting can be scrutinized more closely to detect any tampering. In the case of checks, for instance, if someone attempts to alter the amount, the difference in handwriting style or the presence of a forgery could be quickly identified, thereby reducing the risk of fraudulent transactions.

qa_pairs.question: What steps could the plaintiff have taken to avoid being held liable for a forged endorsement on a negotiable instrument?
qa_pairs.answer: To avoid liability for a forged endorsement on a negotiable instrument, the plaintiff could have taken several precautionary measures. Firstly, the plaintiff should have maintained proper records of endorsements and ensure that all endorsements were made in his presence or through a reliable method such as a notarized endorsement. Secondly, he could have required the use of a signature guarantee stamp from a bank or other financial institution when endorsing the instrument to another party. Thirdly, implementing a strict verification process for endorsements, such as cross-checking the endorsements against the original signature samples kept on file, would help in identifying any forgeries. Additionally, using advanced security features on negotiable instruments, like watermarks, microprinting, or holograms, could also deter forgers. Lastly, staying vigilant and regularly reviewing the status of outstanding checks and other negotiable instruments could help in promptly identifying and addressing any potential issues related to unauthorized endorsements.

Definitions, Rights, and Liabilities 
Transfer means physical delivery of any instrument—negotiable or not—intending to pass title. Section 
3-203(a) of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) provides that “an instrument is transferred when it is 
delivered by a person other than its issuer for the purpose of giving to the person receiving delivery the 
right to enforce the instrument.” 
 
Negotiation and Holder 
Section 3-201(a) of the UCC defines negotiation as “a transfer of possession, whether voluntary or 
involuntary, of an instrument to a person who thereby becomes its holder if possession is obtained from a 
person other than the issuer of the instrument.” A holder is defined in Section 1-201(2) as “a person who 
is in possession of an instrument drawn, issued, or indorsed to him or his order or to bearer or in blank” 
(“in blank” means that no indorsement is required for negotiation). The original issuing or making of an 
instrument is not negotiation, though a holder can be the beneficiary of either a transfer or a negotiation. 
The Official Comment to 3-201(a) is helpful: 
 
A person can become holder of an instrument when the instrument is issued to that person, or the 
status of holder can arise as the result of an event that occurs after issuance. “Negotiation” is the 
term used in article 3 to describe this post-issuance event. Normally, negotiation occurs as the 
result of a voluntary transfer of possession of an instrument by a holder to another person who 
becomes the holder as a result of the transfer. Negotiation always requires a change in possession 
of the instrument because nobody can be a holder without possessing the instrument, either

qa_pairs.question: What does the term 'transfer' mean according to Section 3-203(a) of the Uniform Commercial Code?
qa_pairs.answer: According to Section 3-203(a) of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), a transfer means the physical delivery of any instrument—whether it is negotiable or not—and intending to pass title. qa_pairs.question: How is 'negotiation' defined under the UCC, and what are the conditions for a person to become a holder of an instrument?
qa_pairs.answer: Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), negotiation is defined as a transfer of possession, whether voluntary or involuntary, of an instrument to a person who thereby becomes its holder if possession is obtained from a person other than the issuer of the instrument. A holder is a person who is in possession of an instrument drawn, issued, or indorsed to him or his order or to bearer or in blank. To become a holder, a person must possess an instrument that runs to her, meaning they must have actual possession of the instrument, either directly or through an agent. Furthermore, negotiation always requires a change in possession of the instrument, as nobody can be a holder without possessing the instrument.

Warranty Liability 
The transferor’s contract liability is limited. It applies only to those who sign and only if certain additional 
conditions are met and, as will be discussed, can even be disclaimed. Consequently, a holder who has not 
been paid often must resort to a suit based on one of five warranties. These warranties are implied by law; 
UCC, Section 3-416, details them: 
 
(A) A person who transfers an instrument for consideration warrants all of the following to the 
transferee and, if the transfer is by indorsement, to any subsequent transferee: 
(1) The warrantor is a person entitled to enforce the instrument. 
(2) All signatures on the instrument are authentic and authorized. 
(3) The instrument has not been altered. 
(4) The instrument is not subject to a defense or claim in recoupment of any party which can be 
asserted against the warrantor. 
(5) The warrantor has no knowledge of any insolvency proceeding commenced with respect to 
the maker or acceptor or, in the case of an unaccepted draft, the drawer. 
 
Breach of one of these warranties must be proven at trial if there is no general contract liability. 
 
Liability of Transferees 
The transferee takes by assignment; as an assignee, the new owner of the instrument has only those rights 
held by the assignor. Claims that could be asserted by third parties against the assignor can be asserted 
against the assignee. A negotiable instrument can be transferred in this sense without being negotiated. A 
payee, for example, might fail to meet all the requirements of negotiation; in that event, the instrument 
might wind up being merely transferred (assigned). When all requirements of negotiability and 
negotiation have been met, the buyer is a holder and may (if a holder in due course—see Chapter 21 
"Holder in Due Course and Defenses") collect on the instrument without having to prove anything more. 
But if the instrument was not properly negotiated, the purchaser is at most a transferee and cannot collect 
if defenses are available, even if the paper itself is negotiable.

qa_pairs.question: What are the five warranties that a transferor warrants when transferring an instrument under UCC, Section 3-416, and what must be proven to show a breach of these warranties?
qa_pairs.answer: Under UCC, Section 3-416, a transferor warrants the following five warranties when transferring an instrument: (A) The warrantor is a person entitled to enforce the instrument, (2) All signatures on the instrument are authentic and authorized, (3) The instrument has not been altered, (4) The instrument is not subject to a defense or claim in recoupment of any party which can be asserted against the warrantor, and (5) The warrantor has no knowledge of any insolvency proceeding commenced with respect to the maker or acceptor or, in the case of an unaccepted draft, the drawer. If there is no general contract liability, a breach of one of these warranties must be proven at trial.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a holder and a transferee in the context of negotiable instruments, and how does the process of negotiation affect their rights and obligations?
qa_pairs.answer: In the context of negotiable instruments, a holder is someone who holds the instrument and may be a holder in due course, which means they can collect on the instrument without having to prove anything more, especially if they meet the criteria of a holder in due course as outlined in Chapter 21. On the other hand, a transferee is someone who acquires the instrument through an assignment and does not necessarily have the same rights as a holder. The process of negotiation can significantly affect their rights and obligations. For instance, if the instrument is properly negotiated, the buyer becomes a holder and can collect on the instrument without proving anything further, even if the paper itself is negotiable. However, if the instrument was not properly negotiated, the purchaser is at most a transferee and cannot collect if defenses are available, regardless of whether the paper itself is negotiable.

Sometimes an indorser adds words intended to strengthen the indorsement; for example, “I hereby assign

words of condition, waiver, guaranty, limitation, or disclaimer of liability do not negate the effect of an

Misspelled or Incorrect Indorsements 
When the instrument is made payable to a person under a misspelled name (or in a name other than his 
own), he may indorse in the wrong name or the right one or both. It is safer to sign in both names, and the 
purchaser of the instrument may demand a signature in both names (UCC, Section 3-204(d)). 
 
Various Indorsements and Their Effects 
A holder can indorse in a variety of ways; indorsements are not identical and have different effects. 
 
No Indorsement 
If the instrument requires a signature, transfer without indorsement is an assignment only. Bearer paper 
does not require indorsement, so it can be negotiated simply by delivering it to the transferee, who 
becomes a holder. The transferor has no contract liability on the instrument, however, because he has not 
signed it. He does remain liable on the warranties, but only to the person who receives the paper, not to 
subsequent transferees.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of the 'clear band' on the back of a check, and what happens if it is intruded upon?
qa_pairs.answer: The 'clear band' on the back of a check serves as a designated area that prevents any magnetic (machine-readable) printing from being placed there, ensuring that the front side of the check remains clear for machine reading purposes by banks. This regulation ensures that the rightful owner of the instrument can prove their ownership through either name, thereby safeguarding against potential disputes or fraud. It is safer for the indorser to sign in both names to avoid any complications in transferring the instrument.

qa_pairs.answer: The rule implies that if the indorsement is effective, meaning it was done in good faith by someone paying the instrument or taking it for value or for collection, the drawee bank was justified in debiting the company's account. qa_pairs.question: How do the revised UCC sections affect the application of the fictitious payee defense in cases of bank fraud, according to the text?
qa_pairs.answer: The revised UCC sections, specifically Sections 3-404 and 3-405, introduce the principle of comparative fault, which means that the fictitious payee defense no longer solely protects the depositary bank. Under these revisions, the bank’s own negligence can be considered by the trier of fact, thus undermining the effectiveness of the fictitious payee defense. This change in law means that Wachovia, as the depositary bank, cannot rely solely on the fictitious payee defense to absolve itself of liability in cases where it has engaged in negligent practices.

qa_pairs.question: If Daniel's paycheck was stolen and cashed while he was filling out a deposit slip at the bank, whose financial loss would typically be considered under banking law principles?
qa_pairs.answer: Under banking law principles, the primary loss would generally fall on the drawer (Daniel) rather than the bank. This is because the drawer is responsible for safeguarding their checks until they are deposited. However, the bank might have some responsibility if it failed to take reasonable security measures to prevent theft during the transaction process. To avoid such losses, individuals should ensure that checks are properly secured and completed in a secure environment, ideally in the presence of bank staff to minimize the risk of theft.

qa_pairs.question: What potential liabilities arise when a bank accepts a check with an indorsement that transfers the funds to an estate, but later learns that the funds were misappropriated by the executor?
qa_pairs.answer: When a bank accepts a check with an indorsement transferring funds to an estate and subsequently discovers that the funds were misused by the executor, the bank may face potential liabilities. The bank could be held liable if it knew or should have known about the executor's misconduct and still processed the check. However, if the bank acted in good faith and followed standard procedures, it may be able to limit its liability. Banks must exercise due diligence in verifying the legitimacy of the indorsement and the identity of the person presenting the check. qa_pairs.question: How did the court differentiate between the pre-1990 UCC Article 3 and the post-1990 UCC Article 3 (adopted in Ohio in 1994), particularly regarding the concept of 'good faith'?
qa_pairs.answer: The court noted a significant difference between the pre-1990 UCC Article 3 and the post-1990 UCC Article 3, especially concerning the interpretation of 'good faith.' Pre-1990, 'good faith' was more broadly interpreted, allowing holders to claim holder-in-due-course status even if they did not exercise due diligence. However, the post-1990 Article 3, as adopted in Ohio, placed a stronger emphasis on commercially reasonable actions. It required holders to demonstrate both honesty in fact and to act in a commercially reasonable manner to establish good faith. This meant that simply being honest was no longer sufficient; holders needed to take appropriate steps to ensure the validity of the instrument before claiming holder-in-due-course status.

1. Recognize what a signature is under Article 3 of the Uniform Commercial Code. 
2. Understand how a person’s signature on an instrument affects liability if the person is an agent, or a

The liability of an agent who signs commercial paper is one of the most frequently litigated issues in this 
area of law. For example, Igor is an agent (treasurer) of Frank N. Stein, Inc. Igor signs a note showing that 
the corporation has borrowed $50,000 from First Bank. The company later becomes bankrupt. The 
question: Is Igor personally liable on the note? The unhappy treasurer might be sued by the bank—the 
immediate party with whom he dealt—or by a third party to whom the note was transferred (see Figure 
22.1 "Signature by Representative").

There are two possibilities regarding an agent who signs commercial paper: the agent was authorized to 
do so, or the agent was not authorized to do so. First, though, what is a signature? 
 
A “Signature” under the Uniform Commercial Code 
Section 3-401 of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) provides fairly straightforwardly that “a signature 
can be made (i) manually or by means of a device or machine, and (ii) by the use of any name, including 
any trade or assumed name, or by any word, mark, or symbol executed or adopted by a person with the 
present intention to authenticate a writing.” 
 
Liability of an Agent Who Has Authority to Sign 
Agents often sign instruments on behalf of their principals, and—of course—because a corporation’s 
existence is a legal fiction (you can’t go up and shake hands with General Motors), corporations can only 
act through their agents.

qa_pairs.question: What conditions must be met for an agent's signature on commercial paper to not hold them personally liable?
qa_pairs.answer: An agent's signature on commercial paper generally does not hold them personally liable if they have actual authority to sign the document. This means that the agent had explicit permission from the principal to sign the paper. However, if the agent acts outside the scope of their authority or fraudulently represents themselves as having authority when they do not, they may still be held personally liable. In such cases, the agent could face legal action from either the immediate party with whom they dealt or a subsequent transferee of the note. The key is that the agent must have genuine authority to act on behalf of the principal to avoid personal liability.

By signing a promissory note, the maker promises to pay the instrument—that’s the maker’s contract and, 
of course, the whole point to a note. The obligation is owed to a person entitled to enforce the note or to 
an indorser that paid the note. [2] 
Acceptor 
Recall that acceptance is the drawee’s signed engagement to honor a draft as presented. The drawee’s 
signature on the draft is necessary and sufficient to accept, and if that happens, the drawee as acceptor is 
primarily liable. The acceptance must be written on the draft by some means—any means is good. The 
signature is usually accompanied by some wording, such as “accepted,” “good,” “I accept.” When a 
bank certifies a check, that is the drawee bank’s acceptance, and the bank as acceptor becomes liable to 
the holder; the drawer and all indorsers prior to the bank’s acceptance are discharged. So the holder—
whether a payee or an indorsee—can look only to the bank, not to the drawer, for payment. [3] If the 
drawee varies the terms when accepting the draft, it is liable according to the terms as varied. [4] 
 
Liability of Secondary Parties 
Unlike primary liability, secondary liability is conditional, arising only if the primarily liable party fails to 
pay. The parties for whom these conditions are significant are the drawers and the indorsers. By virtue of 
UCC Sections 3-414 and 3-415, drawers and indorsers engage to pay the amount of an unaccepted draft to 
any subsequent holder or indorser who takes it up, again, if (this is the conditional part) the (1) the 
instrument is dishonored and, in some cases, (2) notice of dishonor is given to the drawer or indorser. 
 
Drawer’s Liability 
If Carlos writes (more properly “draws”) a check to his landlord for $700, Carlos does not expect the 
landlord to turn around and approach him for the money: Carlos’s bank—the drawee—is supposed to pay 
from Carlos’s account. But if the bank dishonors the check—most commonly because of insufficient funds 
to pay it—then Carlos is liable to pay according to the instrument’s terms when he wrote the check or, if it

qa_pairs.question: What role does the maker play in a promissory note and what happens if the maker fails to fulfill their promise?
qa_pairs.answer: The maker in a promissory note is the party who signs the document promising to pay the instrument, which is essentially their contract. The obligation created by the maker is owed to a person entitled to enforce the note or an indorser who has paid the note. If the maker fails to fulfill their promise, the holder of the note can seek enforcement from the maker, or from any subsequent indorser who has paid the note, provided they have taken up the instrument. This means the maker remains responsible until the debt is settled or the note is honored.

qa_pairs.question: How does the acceptance process work for a draft and what are the implications for the parties involved?
qa_pairs.answer: Acceptance of a draft involves the drawee, who is typically a bank or another financial institution, signing the draft to confirm their willingness to pay the amount specified when the draft is presented for payment. The drawee’s signature on the draft is both necessary and sufficient to accept it, and once accepted, the drawee becomes primarily liable for the payment. The acceptance can be indicated by any means, such as writing 'accepted,' 'good,' or 'I accept' on the draft. Importantly, when a bank accepts a check, it assumes the primary liability, and the drawer and any previous indorsers are discharged from responsibility. This means the holder of the draft can look solely to the accepting party for payment, enhancing the security of the transaction. Additionally, if the drawee modifies the terms during acceptance, they become liable according to those new terms, emphasizing the importance of clear communication and agreement between parties.

qa_pairs.question: What legal action can the original owner take when their instrument is converted by a thief who forges an endorsement?
qa_pairs.answer: When an instrument is converted by a thief who forges an endorsement, the original owner, in this case, A, can take legal action for conversion. Since A is the owner of the check and B never obtained rights in the check, A has a cause of action for conversion. The fact that B did not receive the check and thus cannot enforce any obligations related to it does not affect A's claim. Therefore, A can sue the thief for the value of the check and seek damages for the conversion.

qa_pairs.question: What are the five warranties a transferor of a negotiable instrument makes to the transferee and under what conditions do these warranties apply?
qa_pairs.answer: A transferor of a negotiable instrument makes five warranties to the transferee: (1) the transferor is entitled to enforce the instrument, (2) the signatures on the instrument are authentic and authorized, (3) there has been no alteration of the instrument, (4) there are no defenses against the instrument, and (5) the transferor had no knowledge of the drawer's insolvency. If the transfer is made by delivery, these warranties apply only to the immediate transferee. However, if the transfer is made by indorsement, the warranties extend to any subsequent good-faith holder. Additionally, presenters who obtain payment of an instrument and all prior transferors make three presenter’s warranties: (1) they are entitled to enforce the instrument, (2) there has been no alteration of the instrument, and (3) the drawer’s signature is genuine. These warranties also run to any good-faith payor or acceptor.

qa_pairs.question: Under what circumstances might a bank be unable to recover funds when a check is mistakenly paid due to insufficient funds in the drawer's account?
qa_pairs.answer: A bank may be unable to recover funds when a check is mistakenly paid due to insufficient funds in the drawer's account because the person receiving payment of the check (in this case, the bank) will generally have provided value for it in good faith. According to the Uniform Commercial Code, if a bank mistakenly pays a check because the drawer does not have sufficient funds, the bank typically cannot seek reimbursement from the recipient of the check (Baker in the example) once the check has been deposited and processed. Instead, the bank must pursue the drawer (Able in the example) to recover the amount paid out. This rule applies because the recipient of the check has acted in good faith and provided value for the instrument, thus limiting the remedies available to the bank in such situations.

qa_pairs.question: What happens when the holder assents to an acceptance that varies the terms of a draft and how does this affect the obligors?
qa_pairs.answer: When the holder assents to an acceptance that varies the terms of a draft, the obligation of the drawer and any indorsers who do not expressly assent to the acceptance is discharged. Once these words are indorsed on a check, only a bank may acquire the rights of a holder. However, this restriction can be lifted if the check is returned to the customer who initiated the collection process, or if the bank specifically indorses the check to someone who is not a bank. Because EFT is a technology consisting of several discrete types of machines with differing purposes, its 
growth has not been guided by any single law or even set of laws. The most important law governing 
consumer transactions is the Electronic Fund Transfer Act of 1978, [1] whose purpose is “to provide a 
basic framework establishing the rights, liabilities, and responsibilities of participants in electronic fund 
transfer systems. The primary objective of [the statute], however, is the provision of individual consumer 
rights.” This federal statute has been implemented and supplemented by the Federal Reserve Board’s 
Regulation E, Comptroller of the Currency guidelines on EFT, and regulations of the Federal Home Loan 
Bank Board. (Wholesale transactions are governed by UCC Article 4A, which is discussed later in this 
chapter.) 
 
The EFT Act of 1978 is primarily designed to disclose the terms and conditions of electronic funds 
transfers so the customer knows the rights, costs and liabilities associated with EFT, but it does not 
embrace every type of EFT system. Included are “point-of-sale transfers, automated teller machine 
transactions, direct deposits or withdrawal of funds, and transfers initiated by telephone or computer” 
(EFT Act Section 903(6)). Not included are such transactions as wire transfer services, automatic 
transfers between a customer’s different accounts at the same financial institution, and “payments made 
by check, draft, or similar paper instrument at electronic terminals” (Reg. E, Section 205.2(g)). 
 
Consumer Protections Afforded by the Act 
Four questions present themselves to the mildly wary consumer facing the advent of EFT systems: (1) 
What record will I have of my transaction? (2) How can I correct errors? (3) What recourse do I have if a 
thief steals from my account? (4) Can I be required to use EFT? The EFT Act, as implemented by 
Regulation E, answers these questions as follows.

It aims to ensure that consumers are aware of the terms and conditions of electronic funds transfers, including their rights, costs, and liabilities associated with EFT systems.

Definition of Finance
Finance is the study of the management, movement, and raising of money. The word finance can be used as a
verb, such as when the First National Bank agrees to finance your home mortgage loan. It can also be used as
a noun referring to an entire industry. At its essence, the study of finance is about understanding the uses and
sources of cash, as well as the concept of risk-reward trade-off. Finance is also a tool that can help us be better
decision makers.
Basic Areas in Finance
Finance is divided into three primary areas in the domestic market: business finance, investments, and
financial markets and institutions (see Figure 1.2). We look at each here in turn.
Figure 1.2 The Three Basic Areas of Study in Finance
Business Finance
Business finance looks at how managers can apply financial principles to maximize the value of a firm in a
risky environment. Businesses have many stakeholders. In the case of corporations, the shareholders own the

The plan allowed the firm to expand as needed, ensuring they had the necessary capital to manufacture and deliver high-quality products on time and under budget. Without this planning and access to capital, Bacon Signs might not have been able to leverage their strengths in producing superior signs for national franchises. This strategic approach enabled the firm to grow its reputation and meet increasing demand, demonstrating the importance of proper financial planning in business expansion.

Business finance focuses on applying financial principles to maximize the value of a firm in a risky environment. This involves understanding the uses and sources of cash, as well as the risk-reward trade-off. The definition highlights the importance of finance as a tool for making informed decisions, which is essential for managers in optimizing the firm's value. By studying finance, individuals can better understand the financial aspects of running a business, including investment strategies, capital allocation, and risk management, all of which are critical components of business finance.

Capital structure is the process by which managers focus more specifically on long-term debt and

economists, lenders, underwriters, investment bankers, and other sources of external financial

Figure 1.3 demonstrates how the three essential decision-making activities of the financial manager are

Investments
Investments are products and processes used to create and grow wealth. Most commonly, investment topics
include the discussion and application of the different types of financial instruments, delivery vehicles,
regulation, and risk-and-return opportunities. Topics also include a discussion of stocks, bonds, and derivative
securities such as futures and options. A broad coverage of investment instruments would include mutual
funds, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and investment vehicles such as 401k plans or individual retirement
accounts (IRAs). In addition, real assets such as gold, real estate, and commodities are also common
discussion topics and investment opportunities.
Investments is the most interesting area of finance for many students. Television programs such as Billions
and movies such as Wall Street make investing appear glamorous, dangerous, shady, or intoxicating,

business investment decisions, and many students reading this material will work in the investment industry
as personal investment advisers, investment analysts, or portfolio managers.

The overall uncertainty of returns has several components.
•
Default risk on a financial security is the chance that the issuer will fail to make the required payment. For
example, a homeowner may fail to make a monthly mortgage payment, or a corporation may default on
required semiannual interest payments on a bond.
•
Inflation risk occurs when investors have less purchasing power from the realized cash flows from an
investment due to rising prices or inflation.
•
Diversifiable risk, also known as unsystematic risk, occurs when investors hold individual securities or
smallish portfolios and bear the risk that a larger, more well-rounded portfolio could eliminate. In these
situations, investors carry additional risk or uncertainty without additional compensation.
•
Non-diversifiable risk, or systematic risk, is what remains after portfolio diversification has eliminated
unnecessary diversifiable risk. We measure non-diversifiable risk with a statistical term called beta.
Subsequent chapters on risk and return provide a more in-depth discussion of beta.
•
Political risk is associated with macroeconomic issues beyond the control of a company or its managers.
This is the risk of local, state, or national governments “changing the rules” and disrupting firm cash
flows. Political risk could come about due to zoning changes, product liability decisions, taxation, or even
nationalization of a firm or industry.

qa_pairs.question: What are the different types of risks involved in investments and how do they affect the expected return of a security?
qa_pairs.answer: There are several types of risks involved in investments, including default risk, inflation risk, diversifiable risk, non-diversifiable risk, and political risk. Default risk refers to the possibility that the issuer of a financial security will fail to make the required payment, such as a homeowner failing to make a monthly mortgage payment or a corporation defaulting on required interest payments on a bond. Inflation risk is the risk that the purchasing power of the realized cash flows from an investment will decrease due to rising prices. Diversifiable risk, also known as unsystematic risk, arises when investors hold individual securities or smallish portfolios and bear the risk that a larger, more well-rounded portfolio could eliminate. Non-diversifiable risk, or systematic risk, is what remains after portfolio diversification has eliminated unnecessary diversifiable risk, and it is measured using a statistical term called beta. Lastly, political risk is the risk of local, state, or national governments changing the rules and disrupting firm cash flows, which could be caused by zoning changes, product liability decisions, taxation, or even nationalization of a firm or industry. These risks collectively contribute to the overall uncertainty of returns, and understanding them can help investors estimate the range and likelihood of higher- or lower-than-expected outcomes and determine appropriate prices that satisfy investors' required return premiums based on quantifiable expectations about risk or uncertainty.

1.2 The Role of Finance in an Organization
The accounting department creates financial statements, and the finance department implements the firm’s
policy objectives, monitors results, and responds to necessary strategic and tactical changes. Finance is
responsible for budgeting and forecasting. Finance aids in establishing firm objectives and is responsible for
meeting with creditors, lenders, owners, regulators, and other stakeholders that provide capital to the firm or
have a claim against firm assets.
1.3 Importance of Data and Technology
Much of the data used in business today has been available for many years. However, data today is more
attainable than ever due to technological advancements facilitating a user’s ability to gather, evaluate, and
store information faster and more cost effectively than ever. Information is continually available, so the
quicker and less expensively firms can adjust to the arrival of new information, the more valuable they become
for their stakeholders.
1.4 Careers in Finance
Careers in finance are plentiful, fulfilling, and well compensated. Introductory positions are available in areas
such as data collection and data entry. More skill and experience is required for roles such as data analysis and
forecasting. Eventually, executive-level positions such as CFO present themselves to the most qualified.
Finance careers are not limited to financial firms, as understanding finance is an important skill in government
regulatory positions, nonprofit management, and all types of commercial business—from real estate, to retail,
to manufacturing, to education.
1.5 Markets and Participants
Financial markets are where buyers and sellers of financial securities come together to trade. The trading of
securities allows markets to value assets and signal value as new information arrives. Brokers operate to bring
buyers and sellers together and receive commissions. Dealers trade from their own portfolios and are often
willing to make markets for specific securities by agreeing to buy or sell at the current bid and ask prices.
Financial intermediaries actually change or create new financial products.
1.6 Microeconomic and Macroeconomic Matters
Economics is the study of the allocation of scarce resources. Economists attempt to understand the how and
why of human, physical, and financial capital allocation. Microeconomics is the study of factors affecting an
individual’s consumption, and macroeconomics is the study of all the aggregate factors affecting an economy.

qa_pairs.question: What responsibilities does the finance department have in an organization?

It is also responsible for budgeting and forecasting, aiding in the establishment of firm objectives. Additionally, finance departments handle interactions with various stakeholders including creditors, lenders, owners, regulators, and other parties that provide capital to the firm or have claims against its assets.

This increased speed and efficiency allow companies to adapt quickly to new information, making them more valuable to their stakeholders. As a result, the ability to leverage data effectively has become increasingly critical for business success in today's fast-paced environment.

qa_pairs.question: What are municipal bonds and what are their characteristics compared to corporate bonds?
qa_pairs.answer: Municipal bonds (munis) are long-term debt obligations issued by state or local governments that often have important tax advantages relative to corporate bonds. These bonds are typically considered low-risk and liquid, allowing investors to manage short-term financial portfolios of securities easily. Unlike corporate bonds, municipal bonds may offer tax-exempt interest income, making them attractive to investors seeking to minimize their tax liability while earning stable returns.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a negotiable certificate of deposit and a regular certificate of deposit, and how does it trade in the secondary market?
qa_pairs.answer: A negotiable certificate of deposit, also referred to as a jumbo CD, is a very large CD issued by financial institutions that can be redeemed only at maturity but often trades in a broad secondary market. They typically sell in increments of $100,000 or more. In contrast, a regular certificate of deposit has a fixed term and is not typically traded in the secondary market once purchased. The key difference lies in the liquidity and size: while regular CDs are more common and smaller in denomination, negotiable CDs provide more flexibility and higher liquidity due to their large size and ability to trade prior to maturity.

qa_pairs.question: What is the primary issue faced by corporations in the United States related to income taxes and how does the S corporation address this problem?
qa_pairs.answer: The primary issue faced by corporations in the United States is income tax, specifically the phenomenon known as double taxation. Corporate earnings are first taxed at the corporate level, and then the dividends paid to shareholders are taxed again as personal income. To address this issue, the S corporation was introduced by Congress. Unlike regular corporations, S corporations are taxed as if they were proprietorships or partnerships, meaning they are exempt from corporate income tax. This structure helps small businesses avoid the double taxation issue, making it more attractive for relatively small, privately owned firms.

Summary
3.1 Microeconomics
Microeconomics is the study of individual economic decision makers. In the marketplace, buyers and sellers
come together. The buyers are represented by a downward-sloping demand curve; lower prices are associated
with a larger quantity demanded. The sellers are represented by an upward-sloping supply curve; higher
prices are associated with a large quantity supplied. The point of intersection of the supply and demand curves
determines the equilibrium price and quantity.
3.2 Macroeconomics
Macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole. It focuses on broad issues such as inflation,
unemployment, and growth of production. The consumer price index is a common measure of inflation.
Unemployment equals the percent of the labor force that is without a job but looking for work. Gross domestic
product is a measure of the growth of production and growth of the economy.
3.3 Business Cycles and Economic Activity
The business cycle is the repeated pattern of the economy experiencing expansion, a peak, contraction, and a
trough. During the expansion, the economy is growing and real GDP is rising. During a contraction, also
known as a recession, the economy is slowing down.
3.4 Interest Rates
The interest rate is the rental price of money. The nominal interest rate is the quoted, or stated, rate of
interest. The real rate of interest equals the nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate. Lenders charge a
risk premium to compensate them for lending to higher-risk borrowers.

qa_pairs.question: How does microeconomics differ from macroeconomics in terms of scope and focus?
qa_pairs.answer: Microeconomics and macroeconomics differ significantly in their scope and focus. Microeconomics focuses on the behavior of individual economic units, such as households and firms, and how they make decisions in markets. It examines the interactions between buyers and sellers, using concepts like demand and supply curves to determine market outcomes, including the equilibrium price and quantity. On the other hand, macroeconomics takes a broader view of the entire economy, analyzing aggregate measures such as inflation, unemployment, and gross domestic product (GDP) growth. Macroeconomics aims to understand the overall performance of the economy, including its fluctuations over time, known as business cycles, and the factors that influence these broader economic trends.

qa_pairs.question: What happens when the remaining book value of an asset reaches the estimated salvage value during the depreciation process using the double-declining-balance method?
qa_pairs.answer: When the remaining book value of an asset reaches the estimated salvage value during the depreciation process using the double-declining-balance method, the depreciation expense is adjusted to ensure that the asset's book value does not fall below the salvage value. For instance, if in year four, the remaining book value of the asset is $12,528 and the depreciation rate is 40%, attempting to apply the full 40% would result in a depreciation expense of $5,011.20. However, since the salvage value is set at $10,000, the maximum allowable depreciation expense is limited to the difference between the book value and the salvage value, which is $2,528. Thus, the depreciation expense for year four is capped at $2,528 to prevent the book value from falling below the salvage value. Consequently, no further depreciation is allowed in subsequent years once the asset's book value equals the salvage value.

qa_pairs.question: How does the total depreciation expense differ between the straight-line and double-declining-balance methods over the depreciable life of an asset, and what is the significance of this difference?
qa_pairs.answer: While both the straight-line and double-declining-balance methods ultimately lead to the same total depreciation expense over the depreciable life of an asset, the distribution of the depreciation expense varies significantly between the two methods. Under the straight-line method, the depreciation expense is evenly distributed across each year of the asset's useful life. In contrast, the double-declining-balance method results in higher depreciation expenses in the early years and lower expenses in the later years. This is because the double-declining-balance method applies a higher depreciation rate initially, which decreases over time as the book value of the asset reduces. Despite these differences in expense patterns, the total depreciation expense accumulated over the asset's life remains the same for both methods, ensuring that the asset's value is fully expensed by the end of its depreciable period. This consistency in total depreciation expense underscores the importance of understanding the chosen depreciation method's impact on financial statements and tax implications.

qa_pairs.question: What does a firm's open line of credit with a bank entail?
qa_pairs.answer: A firm's open line of credit with a bank entails having a flexible borrowing arrangement where the firm can borrow and repay funds from month to month as their cash flow fluctuates. qa_pairs.question: How do common-size statements facilitate the assessment of a company's performance?
qa_pairs.answer: Common-size statements, also known as vertical analysis, transform financial statement items into percentages relative to a base figure, typically net sales for income statements and total assets for balance sheets. This method reveals relationships between different components of the financial statements, enabling a clearer picture of performance trends over time. Moreover, common-size statements make it easier to compare companies of different sizes, as they standardize the comparison by expressing all figures as a proportion of a consistent base. This approach simplifies the evaluation process and enhances the ability to identify strengths and weaknesses in organizational performance across various industries or within the same company over multiple periods.

5.4 The Statement of Owner’s Equity
The statement of owner’s equity is divided by each type of equity the firm has: common stock, preferred stock,
additional paid-in capital, and retained earnings, for example. Beginning balances are provided, and all key
transactions impacting equity are provided in order to show how ending balance were derived. Key
transactions commonly include recording net income or loss, issuing additional stock, and paying out
dividends.
5.5 The Statement of Cash Flows
Under accrual accounting, transactions are recorded when they occur, not necessarily when cash moves. This
creates a timing difference. Net profit, therefore, does not necessarily mean a firm has cash, and a net loss
doesn’t mean they don’t have any cash. To reconcile net income to actual cash flow and see how a firm
generates and uses its funds, a statement of cash flows is prepared. The statement reflects cash flow from
operating activities, financing activities, and investing activities.
5.6 Operating Cash Flow and Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF)
Operating cash flow reflects the cash generated by (or used by) the core business function. Free cash flow to
the firm (FCFF) or simply free cash flow (FCF) is calculated by deducting capital expenditures from operating
cash flow. FCF reflects the cash available to repay debts, pay dividends to shareholders, and contribute to cash
needs for growth.
5.7 Common-Size Statements
Common-size statements are a restatement of the financial statements with all dollar figures restated as a
percentage. On the income statement, each line is restated as a percentage of net sales. On the balance sheet,
each line is restated as a percentage of total assets. Common-size statements are useful for analysis and are
particularly helpful in comparing firms of different sizes.
5.8 Reporting Financial Activity
Publicly traded firms must file company and financial data with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
on a regular basis. Key reports include the quarterly report, called a 10-Q, and the annual report, called a 10-K.

qa_pairs.question: What is required to determine the ending balance of retained earnings and what does it represent?
qa_pairs.answer: To determine the ending balance of retained earnings, it is necessary to consider key transactions that impact equity, such as recording net income or loss, issuing additional stock, and paying out dividends. Retained earnings represent the cumulative amount of profits that a company has reinvested in its business since inception, minus any dividends paid to shareholders. This account is a crucial part of the equity section of the balance sheet, reflecting the portion of the company's earnings that have been kept within the business rather than distributed to shareholders.

qa_pairs.question: How does the statement of cash flows help reconcile net income with actual cash flow and what does it consist of?
qa_pairs.answer: The statement of cash flows is essential for reconciling net income with actual cash flow because it shows the inflows and outflows of cash during a specific period, providing a clearer picture of a firm's liquidity and financial health. It consists of three main sections: cash flow from operating activities, cash flow from investing activities, and cash flow from financing activities. By detailing these components, the statement of cash flows helps investors and analysts understand how changes in working capital, capital expenditures, and financing decisions affect a company's cash position, thus offering a more comprehensive view of the firm's financial performance compared to just looking at net income alone.

qa_pairs.question: How does a company's earnings per share (EPS) change when the number of shares increases faster than net income?
qa_pairs.answer: Earnings per share (EPS) can decline even when a company’s net income increases if the number of shares increases at a higher rate. This is because EPS is calculated by dividing the net income by the average number of outstanding shares. Therefore, if the increase in the number of shares outpaces the growth in net income, the EPS will decrease despite the rise in net income.

qa_pairs.question: Is it ethical for a company like Apple to engage in large-scale stock buybacks during the pandemic, and what factors should investors consider when evaluating earnings per share?
qa_pairs.answer: The ethicality of Apple engaging in large-scale stock buybacks during the pandemic is debatable. While it might benefit current shareholders by potentially increasing earnings per share, it could also be seen as a short-term strategy that may not align with long-term value creation. Investors and analysts should consider several factors when evaluating earnings per share, including the sustainability of the company’s financial position, the impact of buybacks on the overall market, and whether the buybacks are transparent and communicated effectively to stakeholders. Additionally, they should look at the long-term implications of such actions on the company's financial health and future growth potential.

Summary
7.1 Now versus Later Concepts
This section discussed the underlying concepts of the time value of money (TVM). Because it is possible to earn
interest income on cash that you decide to deposit in an investment or an interest-bearing account, money
that you have now or receive sooner will be more valuable to you than the same amount of money received
later.
7.2 Time Value of Money (TVM) Basics
Future value refers to the value that a current amount will eventually grow into at a given interest rate over a
specific period of time. The single-period scenario is one way in which future amounts are calculated.
Compounding, which is interest earned on interest, also affects the future value of money.
7.3 Methods for Solving Time Value of Money Problems
Calculations can be used to determine future and present dollar amounts, discount and growth rates, and
periods of time required for specific growth. Time value of money problems can be solved using mathematical
equations, calculators with financial functions, and spreadsheets. A useful tool for conceptualizing present
value and future value problems is a timeline. A timeline is a visual, linear representation of the timing of
periods and cash flows over a set amount of time.
7.4 Applications of TVM in Finance
The idea of the time value of money is often considered to be the cornerstone concept of the study of finance.
TVM can help investors and savers understand the value of money today relative to its earning potential in the
future. TVM is critical to understanding the effect that inflation has on money and why saving your money
early can help increase the value of your savings dollars by giving them time to grow and outpace the effects
of inflation. Of course, it is important to remember that there will always be possible options that are sacrificed
with every option you decide on and every choice you make.

qa_pairs.question: What does the concept of the time value of money (TVM) primarily help investors and savers understand?
qa_pairs.answer: The concept of the time value of money (TVM) primarily helps investors and savers understand the value of money today relative to its earning potential in the future. This means that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow because the dollar today can be invested to earn interest, thereby increasing its value over time. TVM is crucial for evaluating the impact of inflation on money, as it explains why saving early can significantly increase the value of your savings by allowing them to grow and outpace inflation. It also aids in making informed decisions about whether to invest in higher-yielding accounts or pay off high-interest debts, as the opportunity cost of one choice must be weighed against the benefits of the other.

qa_pairs.question: How does the time value of money affect decision-making when comparing immediate investment opportunities to future savings?
qa_pairs.answer: The time value of money affects decision-making when comparing immediate investment opportunities to future savings by highlighting the trade-offs involved in each choice. qa_pairs.answer: To calculate the sales in 2029, we can use the formula for compound interest: Future Value = Present Value * (1 + Growth Rate)^Number of Years. qa_pairs.question: A US government bond with a face value of $1,000 will mature in six years and carries an interest rate of 8%. What is the present value of this bond if it does not make any coupon payments?
qa_pairs.answer: Since the bond does not make any coupon payments, we can use the present value formula for a single future sum: PV = FV / (1 + r)^n, where PV is the present value, FV is the future value (face value of the bond), r is the interest rate, and n is the number of periods. Substituting the given values, we get: PV = $1,000 / (1 + 0.08)^6 = $1,000 / 1.5869 = $630.17. Therefore, the present value of the bond is approximately $630.17.

qa_pairs.question: What is the formula used to determine the price of a perpetual dividend if the dividend remains constant?
qa_pairs.answer: The formula used to determine the price of a perpetual dividend when the dividend remains constant is PV = C / Rs, where PV is the price of the preferred stock, C is the constant dividend, and Rs is the required rate of return. qa_pairs.question: How does the presence of expected growth in dividends affect the valuation of a perpetual security like a preferred stock?
qa_pairs.answer: The presence of expected growth in dividends affects the valuation of a perpetual security like a preferred stock by altering the formula to account for the growth rate. The formula for a growing perpetuity is PV = C / (Rs - G), where G is the expected growth rate of the dividend. If the preferred stock of Rooney Corporation has an annual dividend of $1.75, a required rate of return of 5.8%, and an expected growth rate of 1.2%, the value of the stock would be calculated as $1.75 / (0.058 - 0.012) = $38.04, reflecting the higher valuation due to the anticipated increase in dividends over time.

qa_pairs.question: What adjustments are needed when converting an annual interest rate to a non-annual period for calculating monthly payments?
qa_pairs.answer: When converting an annual interest rate to a non-annual period for calculating monthly payments, two adjustments are necessary. First, the annual interest rate needs to be divided by the number of periods in a year. Second, the time periods need to be multiplied by the number of periods within a year. For example, for a monthly payment calculation, the annual interest rate is divided by 12 and the time periods are multiplied by 12.

qa_pairs.question: How would you calculate the monthly payment for a three-year car loan of $32,000 at an annual interest rate of 6%?
qa_pairs.answer: To calculate the monthly payment for a three-year car loan of $32,000 at an annual interest rate of 6%, you would adjust the annual interest rate to a monthly rate by dividing 6% by 12, resulting in 0.5%. Then, since there are 36 months in three years, you would use 36 periods in the present value of an annuity formula. By substituting these values into the formula and solving for the payment amount (PYMT), you find that the monthly payment is approximately $973.50.

Yields and Coupon Rates
The two interest rates that we associate with a bond are often confusing to students when they first begin to
work with bonds. The coupon rate is the interest rate printed on the bond; this is only used to determine the
interest or coupon payments. The yield to maturity (YTM) is an interest rate that is used to discount the bond’s
future cash flow. The YTM is derived from the marketplace and is based on the riskiness of future cash flows.
As we have seen when pricing bonds, a bond’s YTM is the rate of return that the bondholder will receive at the
current price if the investor holds the bond to maturity.
Yield to Maturity
As noted above, the market sets this discount rate, or the yield to maturity. The YTM reflects the going rate in
the bond market for this type of bond and the bond issuer’s perceived ability to make the future payments.
Hence, we base the yield on a mutually agreeable price between seller and buyer. The bond market
determines the YTM and the available supply of competing financial assets. By competing against other
available financial assets, the YTM reflects the risk-free rate and inflation, plus such premiums as maturity and
default specific to the issued bond.
The YTM is the expected return rate on the bond held to maturity. How do we determine the bond’s YTM? We
can use our same three trusty methods: equations, a financial calculator, and Microsoft Excel (as shown at the
end of the chapter).

qa_pairs.question: What are the differences between the coupon rate and the yield to maturity (YTM) of a bond, and how are they relevant in bond valuation?
qa_pairs.answer: The coupon rate is the fixed interest rate printed on the bond, which is used to calculate the regular coupon or interest payments. In contrast, the yield to maturity (YTM) is the internal rate of return that equates the present value of the bond's future cash flows (coupon payments and principal repayment) to its current market price. The YTM is determined by the bond market based on various factors, including the bond's credit risk, time to maturity, and the prevailing interest rates. It represents the total return anticipated on a bond if it is held until the maturity date. In bond valuation, the YTM is crucial because it helps investors understand the expected return on their investment and compare different bonds based on their relative risks and maturities.

As we briefly discussed above, a positive or normal yield curve is indicative of the investment community’s
requirements for higher rates of return as financial consideration for assuming the risk of entering into fixed-
income investments, such as the purchase of bond issues. Typically, as a bond term increases, so will the
potential interest rate risk to the bondholder. Therefore, bonds with longer terms will usually carry higher
coupon rates to make returns greater for investors. Additionally, economists have come to believe that a steep
positive yield curve is a sign that investors anticipate relatively high inflation in the future and thus higher
interest rates accompanied by higher investment yields over shorter (inflationary) periods of time.
Normal yield curves are generally observed during periods of economic expansion, when growth and inflation
are increasing. In any expansionary economy, there is a greater likelihood that future interest rates will be
higher than current rates. This tends to occur because investors will anticipate the Fed or the central bank
raising its short-term rates in response to higher inflation rates within the economy.

qa_pairs.question: What characteristics define a flat yield curve and what are some reasons for its occurrence?
qa_pairs.answer: A flat yield curve is characterized by a lack of significant difference between short-term and long-term yields. It is typically not a long-lasting condition and is often seen during transitions from a normal yield curve to an inverted one, or vice versa. A flat yield curve can also occur due to low interest rates or certain types of unconventional monetary policies.

Term risk. Investors will generally demand higher returns for lending funds at fixed interest rates. This is
because doing so exposes them to the risks presented by rising interest rates and the negative impact of
these higher rates on their bond holdings. In a scenario of rising interest rates, investors will find that
their return from lending money through a bond purchase just once, at a fixed interest rate, will be lower

As mentioned above, however, the most common forms of bond risk are interest rate risk and default risk.
Interest Rate Risk
As we have discussed, when interest rates rise, bond values will fall. This is the general concept behind interest
rate risk. Any investor in fixed-income securities (such as bonds) will have to contend with interest rate risk at
one time or another. Interest rate risk is also referred to as market risk and usually increases the longer an
investor maintains a bond investment.
Default Risk
Any time a bond is purchased, the investor is taking a risk that the bond issuer may be late in making
scheduled payments on a bond issue—or, in the worst case, may not be able to make payments at all. This is
the underlying idea behind the concept of default risk.
Because US Treasury securities have the full backing of the government, they are generally considered free of
default risk. However, most corporate bonds will face some possibility of default. Obviously, some bonds and
their issuing companies are riskier in this respect than others.
To assist potential bond investors in understanding some of these risks, bond ratings are regularly published
by a number of organizations to express their assessment of the risk quality of various bond issues. We will
discuss these bond ratings and the companies that issue them next.

qa_pairs.question: What is reinvestment risk and how does it affect bond investors?
qa_pairs.answer: Reinvestment risk is the risk faced by bond investors when their callable bonds are redeemed by the issuer and the proceeds need to be reinvested at lower interest rates. This occurs because if bond issuers have the option to call their bonds back before maturity, they might do so when interest rates decline, forcing bondholders to reinvest the principal at the prevailing lower rates. Consequently, investors could end up earning less income from their reinvestments compared to what they originally anticipated, leading to potential financial losses.

qa_pairs.question: How does term risk influence bond investments and what is the term premium?
qa_pairs.answer: Term risk, also known as duration risk, affects bond investments by increasing the exposure to changes in interest rates over the life of the bond. As the term of a bond extends, the sensitivity to interest rate fluctuations also increases. The term premium is a measure of the additional return required by investors to compensate for the increased duration risk associated with longer-term bonds. It reflects the extra compensation investors demand for tying up their capital for a longer period, which becomes more critical in environments where interest rates are expected to rise. Term risk is particularly significant for investors who hold bonds to maturity, as it impacts the overall return on their investment.

Generating Capital Gains
Many bonds are not held until their maturity dates. Should an investor require funds before maturity, they
have the option to sell them through a broker in the secondary market. When this situation occurs, the
investor may earn a capital gain or experience a capital loss, depending on whether the bond ends up being
sold at a premium (above face value) or at a discount (below face value).
For example, if an investor bought a corporate bond yielding 7% and then the economy changed so that
comparable bonds yielded 10%, the investor would have to lower their price on the original 7% bond until it
also yielded the 10% market rate. Potential investors would not be very likely to buy the bond if they could
simply buy a newly issued bond from an alternate issuer and receive a higher coupon rate.
It is equally possible that prevailing bond rates could fall and an investor could end up selling their bond at a
higher price, thus earning a capital gain.
Bond Laddering as an Investment Strategy
There are several successful strategies for successful bond investments, but perhaps one of the most common
yet ingenious of these strategies is called bond laddering. Bond ladders help investors achieve diversity in
their portfolios and reduce risk while helping maintain regular cash inflows in the form of coupon payments or
interest. In a bond ladder, an investor will divide their total investment dollars among various bonds that
mature at regular intervals, thereby balancing risk and return. An example of a bond ladder would be to
purchase 10 different bonds that have maturities of one year, two years, three years, and so on, all the way
through to 10 years.
When the first bond matures, the investor will purchase a new bond that matures in 10 years to take its place
in the ladder and continue the overall laddering strategy.

less sensitive to risk than longer-term bonds. The longer-term bonds within the ladder will generally provide
higher returns but with higher risk due to such factors as rising interest rates. So, by investing in bonds with

qa_pairs.question: How does bond laddering work as an investment strategy and what are its benefits?
qa_pairs.answer: Bond laddering is an investment strategy where an investor divides their total investment dollars among various bonds that mature at regular intervals, thereby balancing risk and return. An example of a bond ladder would be to purchase 10 different bonds that have maturities of one year, two years, three years, and so on, all the way through to 10 years. When the first bond matures, the investor will purchase a new bond that matures in 10 years to take its place in the ladder and continue the overall laddering strategy. qa_pairs.question: What does the price-to-book (P/B) ratio measure and how do analysts typically interpret it?
qa_pairs.answer: The price-to-book (P/B) ratio measures the market value of a company's stock compared to its net book value, which is derived from the difference between the company's total assets and total liabilities. Analysts often consider a low P/B ratio (less than 1) to indicate that a stock might be undervalued, suggesting that investors could be paying too little for the company's net assets. Conversely, a high P/B ratio (greater than 1) is seen as indicating that a stock might be overvalued. However, this interpretation can vary among market experts, who may argue the opposite. The P/B ratio can be useful for understanding whether a company's net assets are in line with the market price of its stock, but it is generally recommended to compare P/B ratios within the same industry and use them alongside other metrics and analytical approaches for a more comprehensive evaluation.

Many experienced analysts prefer to use the variable (nonconstant) growth DDM because it is a much closer
approximation of businesses’ actual dividend payment policies, making it much closer to reality than other

qa_pairs.question: What is the intrinsic value of Maddox Inc.'s stock if the required rate of return is 8%, given that the company's dividend policy is to increase its dividends at a rate of 5% for four years and then at 3% per year from the fifth year forward?
qa_pairs.answer: To find the intrinsic value of Maddox Inc.'s stock, we need to calculate the present value of the dividends for the first four years and the present value of the dividends starting from the fifth year. For the first four years, the dividends grow at a rate of 5%. For the fifth year and onwards, the dividends grow at a rate of 3%. The dividends for each year are calculated as follows: Year 1: $2.00 * 1.05 = $2.10; Year 2: $2.10 * 1.05 = $2.21; Year 3: $2.21 * 1.05 = $2.32; Year 4: $2.32 * 1.05 = $2.43. After the fourth year, the dividends start growing at a rate of 3% per year. The present value of the dividends for the first four years is calculated using the formula PV = D / (1 + r)^n, where D is the dividend, r is the required rate of return, and n is the number of years. The present value of the dividends for the fifth year and onwards can be calculated using the Gordon growth model formula: P = D5 / (r - g), where D5 is the dividend in the fifth year, r is the required rate of return, and g is the growth rate. The dividend in the fifth year is calculated as $2.43 * 1.03 = $2.50. Plugging in the numbers, we get P = $2.50 / (0.08 - 0.03) = $50.07886. The present value of this amount, discounted back to the present, is $50.07886 / (1 + 0.08)^4 = $35.7870. Adding up the present values of the dividends for the first four years ($1.9444 + $1.8904 + $1.8379 + $1.7869) and the present value of the dividends starting from the fifth year ($35.7870), we get the intrinsic value of the stock, which is $43.2466.

qa_pairs.question: How does the variable growth model differ from the constant growth DDM (Gordon growth model)?
qa_pairs.answer: The variable growth model differs from the constant growth DDM (Gordon growth model) in that it accounts for different growth rates during different periods of a company's life cycle. In contrast to the constant growth model, which assumes a single, unchanging growth rate for all future periods, the variable growth model allows for varying growth rates, reflecting the reality that companies often experience different growth phases. For instance, a company might experience rapid growth during its early stages, followed by a period of slower growth as it matures. This approach provides a more accurate representation of a company's expected dividend payments and, consequently, a more realistic valuation of its stock. The variable growth model calculates the present value of dividends for each growth period separately and then sums these values to determine the total intrinsic value of the stock. While this method is more complex than the constant growth model, it offers a more nuanced and precise assessment of a stock's worth, especially for companies with diverse growth trajectories.
